concepts.title: Profit versus cash
concepts.summary: Profit is earned over a period; cash is what’s in the account now. They drift apart whenever money arrives or leaves at a different time from when work is counted.

concepts.title: When revenue counts
concepts.summary: Revenue belongs to the period the work is delivered, not when it is invoiced or paid. Invoices create receivables; payments turn them into cash.

concepts.title: State the point first
concepts.summary: Lead with the answer, then the reason, then what you need, so a busy listener gets the part they asked for in the first sentence.

concepts.title: The deliberate pause
concepts.summary: A short pause before answering a pointed question signals thought, not evasion, and keeps you from filling silence with background.

concepts.title: Listen for the need
concepts.summary: Say back what the other person needs, not just the words they used, so they can correct you before you solve the wrong problem.
misconceptions: Treats reflecting as repeating the other person’s words, rather than naming what they need.

concepts.title: The layers of an income statement
concepts.summary: How revenue becomes net income, one deduction at a time: direct costs, running costs, then interest and tax.

concepts.title: Gross versus operating margin
concepts.summary: Gross margin shows whether the work is priced well; operating margin shows whether the business pays for itself after overhead.

concepts.title: Federal versus state powers
concepts.summary: Which decisions the Constitution gives to Washington, which it leaves to the states, and where the two collide.

concepts.title: Claims versus evidence
concepts.summary: Separate what someone asserts from what would show it’s true, and ask what evidence would change your mind.

concepts.title: Connecting the week
concepts.summary: Pull separate ideas into one explanation in your own words, the habit behind every portfolio piece.

concepts.title: Assets, liabilities and equity
concepts.summary: What a business owns equals what it owes plus what belongs to its owners, and how that snapshot pairs with the income statement.

concepts.title: The right amount of context
concepts.summary: Give the listener only the background they need to act on your point, and hold the rest until they ask.

concepts.title: Facts versus values
concepts.summary: Tell apart disagreements about what is true from disagreements about what matters, and how Congress, the president and the courts divide power.

concepts.title: The three kinds of cash flow
concepts.summary: Operating, investing and financing cash flows, and why a growing business can burn cash while reporting a profit.

concepts.title: Fixed and variable costs
concepts.summary: Which costs move with each job and which don’t, and how that sets a break-even point.

practice.title: Feedback on a missed deliverable
practice.headline: You named the problem clearly, but let Katie steer the fix instead of agreeing on one.

practice.title: Does rent control help renters?
practice.headline: Strong on supply effects, but you conceded the tenant-stability point without answering it.

practice.title: Explain the 401(k) match
practice.headline: Accurate, but you started with vesting rules before saying why the match is free money.

history.title: Review
history.summary: A quick review of reflective listening. Nathan still restated the client’s complaint instead of naming the need behind it; worth another pass soon.

history.title: Listen, pause, state the point
history.summary: Nathan rewrote a delay update so the point came first and handled the check on it cleanly. He wasn’t sure when a pause helps and asked to be taught. Reflective listening tripped him up: he paraphrased words rather than naming the need, then got it right on a second try.

history.title: Profit versus cash
history.summary: Nathan separated profit from cash in Jake’s video studio, chose the right explanation for a thin bank balance, and applied it to a catering deposit. His first written explanation blamed spending rather than slow collections; the transfer answer fixed that. Revenue timing is new and still shaky.

history.title: How do stock buybacks actually help shareholders?
history.summary: Nathan explored how buybacks return cash to shareholders by shrinking the share count, and why they are not automatically good: price paid matters.
